title: Gulf oil exports are back, but how durable is recovery?
gist: Gulf crude exports excluding Iran rebounded to at least 16.5 million barrels per day in September 2026, back to pre-conflict levels from 6.5 million in March per Kpler, as Iran's grip on Hormuz erodes; yet Brent hovers around $100, still about 40% above pre-war levels, because traders price risk that a weakened Iran escalates attacks elsewhere — a recovery Samuel Wendel argues may prove short-lived.

insights.claim: Gulf crude exports excluding Iran reached at least 16.5 million barrels per day in September 2026, back to pre-conflict levels and up from 6.5 million in March, according to Kpler.
insights.speaker: Samuel Wendel
insights.so_what: Physical Gulf supply has normalized in volume terms, removing much of the outright supply shortfall even as risk premium persists.
insights.quote: Gulf crude exports reached at least 16.5 million barrels per day in September excluding Iran
insights.locator: Gulf crude exports reached at least

insights.claim: The export recovery reflects months of Gulf adaptation of energy logistics and export strategies, alongside stepped-up US military support for shipping.
insights.speaker: Samuel Wendel
insights.so_what: Recovery depends partly on continued US naval protection — a withdrawal of that support would reverse flows.
insights.quote: The recovery reflects months of adaptation by Gulf states
insights.locator: Gulf crude exports reached at least

insights.claim: Despite the export rebound, Brent crude hovered around $100 per barrel, still roughly 40% above pre-war levels.
insights.speaker: Samuel Wendel
insights.so_what: A large risk premium remains embedded; a durable de-escalation could compress Brent substantially, while escalation could spike it.
insights.quote: Brent crude hovered right around $100 per barrel on the news, still up some 40% from pre-war levels
insights.locator: Yet the market has hardly celebrated

insights.claim: Traders keep pricing significant supply risk because they fear Iran will escalate attacks in the Gulf and beyond as its Hormuz leverage weakens.
insights.speaker: Samuel Wendel
insights.so_what: Second-order risk: losing Hormuz leverage may push Iran toward wider, less predictable escalation, so lower chokepoint risk does not mean lower overall risk.
insights.quote: fears that Iran will escalate attacks in the Gulf and beyond as Hormuz leverage weakens
insights.locator: Yet the market has hardly celebrated

insights.claim: What looks like a breakthrough for regional producers may prove less durable than headlines suggest; the crude revival could be short-lived.
insights.speaker: Samuel Wendel
insights.so_what: Caution against extrapolating the September rebound into lower oil prices or sustained Gulf revenue recovery.
insights.quote: what looks like a breakthrough for regional producers may prove less durable than headlines suggest
insights.locator: The US-Iran war reached the seven-month mark

insights.claim: Jim Krane of Rice University's Baker Institute described the situation as fragile and tentative.
insights.speaker: Samuel Wendel
insights.so_what: Expert view reinforces that the rebound is not a settled normalization.
insights.quote: The whole situation feels fragile and tentative
